title: Sleep Debt and High Blood Pressure: What the Studies Show
seoTitle: Sleep Debt and High Blood Pressure: What Studies Show
subtitle: How a lack of rest can affect cardiovascular health
excerpt: Accumulated lack of sleep, called sleep debt, is linked to metabolic and cardiovascular problems, as well as hypertension.
author: Daniele Morais
sourceName: Portal Drauzio Varella, Tua Saúde, Diário do Comércio
contentHtml:
In recent years, the media has brought to light sleep debt, a term that describes the difference between the amount of sleep a person actually gets and the amount they need. This accumulated lack of rest not only impairs memory and learning, but can also increase blood pressure, according to recent research.

Sleep debt: why it is not resolved over the weekend

According to specialist Monica Andersen, director of education and research at the Sleep Institute, “we have no way of paying off this sleep debt on weekends. However, it is better for us to recover some of this debt on weekends than to start Monday with even more hours of sleep owed to our brains.”

Sleep is essential for memory consolidation, hormone regulation, immune response, and maintaining alertness. Sleep deprivation can reduce wakefulness, increase sleepiness, affect mood, and alter the physiological response to stress.

Sleep and blood pressure: what the literature says

During deep sleep, blood pressure naturally drops by 10% to 20% – known as the “nocturnal dip.” When sleep is interrupted, short, or of poor quality, this drop does not happen properly. Sleep deprivation increases sympathetic nervous system activity, raises cortisol, and alters hormones linked to sodium and water balance, contributing to high blood pressure in predisposed individuals.

A meta-analysis titled Subjective sleep quality, blood pressure, and hypertension, published in the Journal of Clinical Hypertension and indexed in PubMed, gathered data from 29 articles involving 45,000 patients. Poor sleep quality was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of hypertension, with hypertensive patients presenting worse sleep quality scores and a lower nocturnal blood pressure dip compared to those considered good sleepers.

Association or causality? What the studies actually show

  • Association indicates that two factors frequently appear together, but does not prove which causes which
  • Causality requires controlled experiments that demonstrate a direct cause-and-effect relationship
  • Confounding factors such as obesity, anxiety, and a sedentary lifestyle can be behind both poor sleep and hypertension
  • Bidirectionality means that high blood pressure can also impair sleep, creating a difficult cycle to break
  • Individuality shows that not every hypertensive person responds the same way to changes in sleep patterns

How to improve sleep to control blood pressure

  1. Maintain regular sleep and wake schedules, including on weekends
  2. Reduce caffeine, alcohol, and screens in the two hours before sleep
  3. Take care of the bedroom environment, keeping it cool, quiet, and dark
  4. Engage in regular physical activity combined with a healthy diet
  5. For shift workers, evaluate light exposure, break distribution, and shift duration, as well as sleep organization strategies

What your body says when you do not get enough sleep

According to Fernanda Carolina Silva Guimarães Cruz, PhD in Sciences from USP, sleep restriction causes changes that are not completely reversed after just two nights of recovery. Sleep debt can increase sleepiness, reactivity to negative stimuli, and irritability, in addition to contributing to weight gain, sexual changes, and even dermatological issues.

For those who need to sleep less during the week, the recommendation is to try to reduce the deficit without making major changes to schedules. The preferred strategy is to go to bed earlier and keep the wake-up time close to usual, avoiding major variations that generate “social jet lag” and increase misalignment between the biological clock and social schedules.

The role of sleep hygiene in overall health

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) and the Sleep Research Society recommend that adults regularly sleep seven hours or more per night to promote health. However, sleep needs vary from individual to individual, and each person may need more or less time to feel well.

In summary, accumulated sleep debt and poor sleep quality are associated with an increased risk of hypertension and other health problems. Improving sleep hygiene, maintaining regular schedules, and taking care of the sleeping environment are fundamental steps to reduce blood pressure and promote overall well-being.

With information from Portal Drauzio Varella, Tua Saúde, Diário do Comércio.
